title: Tail Risk Premia for Long-Term Equity Investors

extraction.methodology_summary: The paper proposes a model-free framework to estimate long-term variance, skewness, and kurtosis risk premia on the S&P 500 using Discretisation-Invariant (DI) moment swaps. These swaps are replicated via static portfolios of out-of-the-money European options and dynamic trading in log contracts. The authors construct 30-day constant-maturity investable P&L series at daily, weekly, and monthly frequencies to analyze the risk premia's statistical properties and their determinants using Fama-French and Carhart factors.

performance_metrics.context: Correlation between the daily changes in the S&P500 forward and the variance swap under daily monitoring
performance_metrics.evidence_quote: the correlation between the daily changes in the S&P500 forward and the variance swap in the top panel is around -0.6

performance_metrics.context: Correlation between the variance and skew risk premiums under monthly monitoring
performance_metrics.evidence_quote: the correlation of -0.86 between the variance and skew risk premiums is in line with Kozhan et al. [2013].

performance_metrics.context: Fama-French and Carhart five-factor regression of the daily changes in the 30-day S&P500 variance risk premium (VRP) over the full sample (1996-2013)
performance_metrics.evidence_quote: The addition of the Fama-French factors only marginally increases the adjusted R2 from 0.567 to 0.581

performance_metrics.context: Regression of the daily changes in the 30-day S&P500 skewness risk premium during the financial crisis period (July 2008 to June 2009) using only market factors
performance_metrics.evidence_quote: and even higher (0.753) for the skewness risk premium.

key_findings: Momentum is the dominant driver for both skewness and kurtosis risk premia, which exhibit a highly significant negative correlation.
The variance risk premium (VRP) responds positively to size and negatively to growth, and is not driven by momentum.
There is a significant asymmetric response of the VRP and other moment risk premia to market shocks when measured at high sampling frequencies (daily).

The correlation between variance and tail risk premia (skewness and kurtosis) is relatively low at high sampling frequencies (around -0.5 and 0.5) compared to monthly frequency (where VRP and skewness correlation is -0.86).
Long-term investors can diversify their exposures to variance risk (driven by growth) and skewness/kurtosis risk (driven by momentum).
limitations: The study does not explicitly incorporate transaction costs for the dynamic replication of the swaps, which could affect the exploitability of the risk premia.
At long-term horizons, there are insufficient non-overlapping time-series data available for highly reliable statistical estimation without spanning across different market regimes.
